newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Mobutu returns home, pledges action.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Mobutu returns home, pledges action.

text.p: President Mobutu Sese Seko has pledged a rapid and positive response to Zaire's crisis after returning home against the advice of doctors treating him following cancer surgery.

But the man who has dominated life in the anarchic Central African nation since seizing power in 1965 gave no specific ideas on how he plans to respond to its problems, notably a Tutsi-led revolt in the east.

"I know your expectations and your hopes. I will devote myself to finding a rapid and positive response in the higher interest of the nation," Mobutu, 66, told supporters after returning from four months in Europe on Tuesday.
The rebels remained defiant. "We know he is preparing a counter-attack, but we are confident and prepared to respond," one spokesman said in Brussels.
Huge crowds turned out to welcome Mobutu, who had been in Europe since August when he had surgery for prostate cancer.
Up to 20,000 people packed Njili international airport outside the capital Kinshasa.
Many tens of thousands more lined his route from the airport through the teeming capital of five million people to his fortified hilltop residence in the Ngaliama district.
"Each time that Zaire has been threatened in the past, I have never pulled back. I will never pull back," he told supporters there in an address broadcast live by state radio.
Many Zaireans look to Mobutu, who arrived from France, to conjure up a solution to end the revolt in the east, where rebels have seized territory and towns.
But there is also widespread disenchantment with formal authority among ordinary Zaireans who are finding it harder and harder to make ends meet.

Mobutu smiled broadly as he walked down the steps from the aircraft with his wife, Bobi Ladawa. Wearing his trademark leopardskin hat, he walked unaided and easily, carrying, as always, a carved walking stick.
Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo waited at the aircraft steps. No opposition personalities were in evidence.
Mobutu, who has held power with a mix of military might and political acumen, bowed to foreign and domestic pressure for democratic reforms in 1990 but elections have yet to be held.

Local newspapers of all political tendencies have speculated on the implications of his return and possible changes in the government and the military. They were sharply divided on whether his presence would make any difference on the war front.
Mobutu, who has been recuperating at his private villa at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin near Nice since November 4, said he was still convalescing, but added:

"I could not remain unmoved in the face of the worsening situation in the east of the county and the appeals, so, against the advice of doctors, I decided to break my stay in France to continue my convalescence in the midst of my people."
